claims.claim: A queue is a collection in which only the earliest added item may be accessed; add is at the tail (enqueue) and delete is at the head (dequeue); it is also known as first-in, first-out (FIFO).

The Queue interface's most common queueing discipline is FIFO, in which the remove operation returns the element that has been in the queue longest; on a FIFO queue the add/remove operations are commonly called enqueue and dequeue.
Appends and pops from either end of a Python collections.deque run with approximately O(1) performance, which makes the deque suitable for implementing a queue.

Removing from or inserting at the front of a plain Python list (pop(0) / insert(0, v)) incurs O(n) memory-movement cost because it changes the position of the underlying data, so a naive array-front implementation of a queue is not O(1).
Enqueuing 1, then 2, then 3 into an empty queue and then dequeuing repeatedly returns 1, 2, 3 in that order, preserving arrival order (FIFO).

A priority queue serves the highest-priority (e.g., smallest) element next rather than the oldest, and a deque (double-ended queue) generalizes the queue by allowing operations at both ends; these are listed as related structures to the queue.
Breadth-first search uses a queue so that nodes discovered earlier are processed before nodes discovered later, producing level-by-level traversal.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the array-based queue operations are strictly O(1) or amortized/approximately O(1).
positions: A linked-list queue with head and tail pointers gives strict worst-case O(1) enqueue/dequeue.

A dynamic circular-array (ArrayQueue) queue gives amortized/approximately O(1) per operation because occasional resizing is O(n) but averages out; Python's deque docs phrase deque ends as 'approximately O(1)'.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states operations are O(1) with a proper implementation and cites the deque docs' 'approximately O(1)' wording; it does not overclaim strict worst-case O(1) for the array variant. The key teaching point - that naive array-front removal is O(n) while a proper implementation is constant-time - holds either way.
